n: The heading sets this when Saul sent men to watch David’s house at night to kill him; David escaped through a window with Michal’s help. He asks God to set him safely out of reach.

f.g: Set me on high, out of reach.

n: He pleads to be saved from evildoers and murderers.
Powerful men lie in ambush for him, though he has done nothing to deserve it.

f.g: David protests his innocence toward Saul.

n: They rush to attack without cause. David asks God to wake up and see what is happening.
He calls on the Lord God of armies to rise up and deal with all the nations and faithless traitors.

f.g: The Lord, commander of heavenly armies.

n: Each evening the attackers return like wild dogs, snarling and prowling around the city. Stray dogs in the ancient Near East were scavengers, not pets.

f.w: make a noise like a dog
f.g: Howl and snarl like pariah dogs.

n: They spew threats, and their words are swords. They think, “Who will hear us?” — as if God isn’t listening.
But God laughs at them — their threats are laughable to him.
David waits for God, his strength and his high fortress.

f.g: A high place of safety, a fortress.

n: God, in his loyal love, will go ahead of him and let him see his enemies defeated.

f.g: In KJV English, “prevent” means go before or meet — not stop.

n: Surprisingly, David asks God not to kill them quickly, lest the people forget the lesson. Let them wander and fall slowly, as a living reminder.
Let their own proud, lying words trap them.
Let all the earth know that God rules in Jacob — Israel — and to the ends of the earth.
The image of the prowling dogs returns as a refrain.
Let them roam about for food and growl when they aren’t satisfied.

f.g: Growl, complain, or stay up all night.

n: In contrast to the howling dogs at night, David will sing in the morning about God’s strength and love. The night of danger ends in a dawn of praise.
The psalm closes with a refrain of trust, calling God his strength, fortress, and loyal God.

f.g: The God who shows me ḥesed — steadfast love.
